hints: Each sprinkler covers one stretch of the lawn. If you are standing at some point that is already watered, what do you want from the next sprinkler you switch on?
Turn it into a jump problem: for every left point l, store the farthest right end any sprinkler starting at or covering from l reaches. Then use the fewest-hops greedy window over the line.

1. best[l] = farthest right end of a sprinkler whose left end (clamped at 0) is l.
  2. Walk i from 0 to n−1, keeping farthest = max(farthest, best[i]).
  3. When i reaches the end of the watered part: if farthest ≤ i, return −1; else count one sprinkler and extend the watered end to farthest.
  4. Return the count.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try all subsets of sprinklers and check which cover [0, n].

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: DP: dp[x] = fewest sprinklers to cover [0, x], updated from every sprinkler's range.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Build best-reach per left point, then a jump-game greedy across the lawn.

explain: In sample 1 (n = 6, reach = [1,0,3,0,0,0,1]), sprinkler 2 covers [−1,5] → clamped left 0, so best[0] = 5; sprinkler 6 covers [5,7] → best[5] = 6. Walking: at i = 0 the watered end is 0 so we switch on the best one (reach 5). Between 1 and 5 farthest grows to 6 thanks to best[5]; at i = 5 we switch on a second one and cover to 6. Answer 2. In sample 2 nothing reaches past point 2, so at that point farthest ≤ i and we return −1. A gap anywhere means it is impossible.
recognize: Cover a whole segment with the fewest given ranges → convert to 'farthest reach from each point' and run the minimum-jumps greedy.
